content.title: Understanding JMeter Test Plans
content.explanation:
**The Blueprint of Your Performance Test:**

**1. What is a Test Plan?**

A Test Plan is the root element of every JMeter test. It's a container that holds all the components needed to execute a performance test – from virtual users and requests to validations and results collection.

```
📋 TEST PLAN = Complete Test Definition
├── Who? (Thread Group - virtual users)
├── What? (Samplers - requests to make)
├── How? (Configuration - settings, data)
├── When? (Timers - pacing, think time)
├── Validation? (Assertions - pass/fail criteria)
└── Results? (Listeners - output collection)
```

**2. Test Plan Components**

| Component | Purpose | Example |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| **Thread Group** | Defines virtual users | 100 users, 60 sec ramp-up, 5 loops |
| **Samplers** | Send requests to server | HTTP Request, JDBC Request, FTP Request |
| **Config Elements** | Set up defaults and variables | HTTP Request Defaults, CSV Data Set |
| **Timers** | Add think time between requests | Constant Timer, Gaussian Random Timer |
| **Pre-Processors** | Run before samplers | User Parameters, JSR223 PreProcessor |
| **Post-Processors** | Run after samplers | Regular Expression Extractor |
| **Assertions** | Validate responses | Response Assertion, Duration Assertion |
| **Listeners** | Collect and display results | View Results Tree, Summary Report |
| **Controllers** | Control test flow | Loop Controller, If Controller |

**3. Test Plan Hierarchy**

```
📋 Test Plan (Root)
├── 📁 Thread Group (User simulation)
│   ├── 🎛️ Config Elements (Setup)
│   ├── 🎯 Samplers (Requests)
│   ├── ⏱️ Timers (Think time)
│   ├── 🔧 Pre/Post Processors (Data handling)
│   ├── ✅ Assertions (Validation)
│   └── 👂 Listeners (Results)
├── 📁 Setup Thread Group (Initialization)
└── 📁 Teardown Thread Group (Cleanup)
```

**4. Test Plan Properties**

```
Key settings at Test Plan level:

Name: [Descriptive name of your test]
Comments: [Purpose, author, date, notes]

✅ User Defined Variables:
- Define global variables for the entire test
- Accessible anywhere in the test plan

✅ Run Thread Groups consecutively:
- If checked, groups run one after another
- If unchecked, all groups start simultaneously

✅ Functional Test Mode:
- Saves more data (slower, use only for debugging)

✅ Add directory or jar to classpath:
- For custom code, JDBC drivers, etc.
```

**5. Creating Your First Test Plan**

```
1. Launch JMeter
2. The default test plan is already created
3. Rename it: Right-click Test Plan → Rename
4. Add comments describing the test purpose
5. Set any global variables if needed
6. Start adding Thread Groups

Test plan file format: .jmx (XML-based)
Save: File → Save (Ctrl+S)
```

**6. Test Plan Best Practices**

```
✅ DO:
- Give descriptive names to all elements
- Use comments to document your test plan
- Save test plan before running
- Keep test plans version controlled (Git)
- Use User Defined Variables for config
- Organize with controllers for reusability

❌ DON'T:
- Run large tests in GUI mode
- Hardcode values that change
- Forget to clear results between runs
- Use too many listeners during load tests
- Ignore assertions (failing silently)
```

**7. Example Test Plan Structure**

```
📋 E-Commerce Load Test
├── 📁 Setup Thread Group (Create test data)
│   └── 🎯 HTTP Request - Create Users
├── 📁 Main Traffic Simulation
│   ├── 🎛️ HTTP Request Defaults
│   │   └── Server: api.example.com
│   ├── 📁 User Journeys
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Homepage
│   │   ├── ⏱️ Constant Timer (think: 2 sec)
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Search Products
│   │   ├── ⏱️ Constant Timer (think: 3 sec)
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Add to Cart
│   │   └── ✅ Response Assertion (200)
│   └── 👂 Listeners
│       ├── 👂 View Results Tree
│       └── 👂 Summary Report
└── 📁 Teardown Thread Group (Clean up)
    └── 🎯 HTTP Request - Delete Test Data
```
```

content.title: Creating and Configuring a Test Plan
Building Your Test Plan from Scratch

steps.action: Configure the root test plan element
details:
**When you first launch JMeter, a default Test Plan is already created.**

**Step-by-step configuration:**

```
1. Select the Test Plan element in the tree
2. In the right panel, configure:

   Name: E-Commerce Performance Test
   Comments: Load test for shopping flow
             Created: 2025-02-20
             Author: Performance Team

3. User Defined Variables (add if needed):
   Click "Add" → "User Defined Variables"
   Add variables like:
   - HOST = api.example.com
   - PROTOCOL = https
   - PORT = 443

4. Check/Uncheck options:
   [ ] Run Thread Groups consecutively
       (leave unchecked for parallel execution)
   [ ] Functional Test Mode
       (keep unchecked for performance)

5. Add to classpath if needed:
   - For JDBC drivers, add JAR path
   - For custom code, add directory
```

**User Defined Variables Example:**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ User Defined Variables              │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Name: HOST    Value: api.example.com│
│ Name: PROTOCOL Value: https         │
│ Name: TIMEOUT Value: 5000           │
│ Name: THREADS Value: 100            │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

These variables can be used anywhere with ${HOST} syntax.
```

**Save your test plan:**
```
File → Save (Ctrl+S)
Save as: ecommerce-load-test.jmx
```

**What you've accomplished:**
- ✓ Named and documented your test plan
- ✓ Set up global variables
- ✓ Saved your test plan

**Thread Group = Virtual Users** – it defines who will run your test.

**Steps to add a Thread Group:**

```
1. Right-click on Test Plan
2. Add → Threads (Users) → Thread Group
3. Select the Thread Group in the tree
4. Configure in right panel:
```

**Thread Group Configuration:**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Thread Group                                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Name: Main Website Users                                    │
│ Comments: Simulates regular website visitors                │
│                                                             │
│ Action to be taken after a Sampler error:                   │
│ ● Continue  ○ Stop Thread  ○ Stop Test  ○ Stop Test Now    │
│ (Choose 'Continue' to see all errors)                       │
│                                                             │
│ Thread Properties:                                          │
│   Number of Threads (users): 100                            │
│   Ramp-up period (seconds): 60                              │
│   Loop Count: 5  [ ] Infinite                               │
│   (100 users over 60 seconds = 1-2 users/second)           │
│                                                             │
│ [ ] Same user on each iteration (use cookies)               │
│ [✓] Delay thread creation until needed                      │
│ [ ] Specify thread lifetime                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Understanding the numbers:**

```
Example: 100 users, 60 sec ramp-up, 5 loops

- Users start: 1-2 new users per second
- After 60 seconds: all 100 users active
- Each user executes the test 5 times
- Total requests = 100 users × 5 loops × samplers per loop

If you have 5 samplers: 100 × 5 × 5 = 2,500 total requests
```

**Different Thread Group types:**

```
📁 Thread Group (regular) – Main test users
📁 Setup Thread Group – Runs before main test (create data, login)
📁 Teardown Thread Group – Runs after main test (cleanup)

Example setup:
- Setup: Create test users (1 thread, 1 iteration)
- Main: 100 users browsing (main test)
- Teardown: Delete test users (1 thread, 1 iteration)
```

**What you've accomplished:**
- ✓ Added a Thread Group
- ✓ Configured users, ramp-up, and loops
- ✓ Understood the load pattern

**HTTP Request Defaults** saves time by setting common values for all HTTP requests.

**Steps to add:**

```
1. Right-click on Thread Group
2. Add → Config Element → HTTP Request Defaults
3. Configure:
```

**HTTP Request Defaults Configuration:**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HTTP Request Defaults                                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Name: API Defaults                                          │
│ Comments: Common settings for all API calls                 │
│                                                             │
│ Web Server:                                                 │
│   Protocol: [https]        (use ${PROTOCOL} variable)      │
│   Server or IP: [api.example.com]  (use ${HOST})           │
│   Port: [443]                                              │
│                                                             │
│ HTTP Request:                                               │
│   Method: [GET] (default, can override)                     │
│   Path: (leave blank, each request sets its own)           │
│                                                             │
│ Parameters: (add common query params)                       │
│   Send Parameters With the Request:                         │
│   - api_key: ${API_KEY} (if all requests need it)          │
│   - version: v2                                             │
│                                                             │
│ Body Data: (usually left blank)                             │
│                                                             │
│ Server Timeouts:                                            │
│   Connect: [5000] (ms)                                      │
│   Response: [10000] (ms)                                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Benefits of HTTP Request Defaults:**

```
✅ Centralized configuration – change once, affect all requests
✅ Cleaner individual requests – only specify what's unique
✅ Easier environment switching – change server in one place
✅ Less duplication – more maintainable test plans

Example: Without defaults, each request would need:
- Protocol: https
- Server: api.example.com
- Port: 443
- Timeout: 5000

With defaults, each request only needs its specific path!
```

**Using variables in defaults:**

```
If you set User Defined Variables at Test Plan level:
- PROTOCOL = https
- HOST = api.example.com

Then in HTTP Request Defaults:
- Protocol: ${PROTOCOL}
- Server: ${HOST}

Now switching environments is as simple as changing variables!
```

**What you've accomplished:**
- ✓ Added HTTP Request Defaults
- ✓ Configured common server settings
- ✓ Set up timeouts
- ✓ Learned to use variables

**HTTP Request Samplers** are the heart of your test – they make the actual requests to your application.

**Steps to add:**

```
1. Right-click on Thread Group
2. Add → Sampler → HTTP Request
3. Configure each request
```

**Example: Homepage Request**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HTTP Request                                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Name: Homepage                                              │
│ Comments: Load homepage                                     │
│                                                             │
│ (Server settings inherited from HTTP Request Defaults)      │
│                                                             │
│ HTTP Request:                                               │
│   Method: GET                                               │
│   Path: /                                                   │
│                                                             │
│ Parameters: (none)                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Example: Product Search Request**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HTTP Request                                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Name: Search Products                                       │
│                                                             │
│ HTTP Request:                                               │
│   Method: GET                                               │
│   Path: /api/products/search                                │
│                                                             │
│ Parameters: (add as table)                                  │
│   q:        laptop                                          │
│   category: electronics                                     │
│   page:     1                                               │
│   limit:    20                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Example: Add to Cart Request (POST)**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HTTP Request                                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Name: Add to Cart                                           │
│                                                             │
│ HTTP Request:                                               │
│   Method: POST                                              │
│   Path: /api/cart/add                                       │
│                                                             │
│ Body Data:                                                  │
│   {"productId": 12345, "quantity": 1, "options": {}}      │
│                                                             │
│ (Don't forget Content-Type header!)                         │
│ Add Headers tab:                                            │
│   Content-Type: application/json                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Example: Login Request (POST with form data)**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HTTP Request                                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Name: Login                                                 │
│                                                             │
│ HTTP Request:                                               │
│   Method: POST                                              │
│   Path: /api/auth/login                                     │
│                                                             │
│ Parameters (use "Parameters" tab for form data):            │
│   username: testuser@example.com                            │
│   password: secret123                                       │
│                                                             │
│ Headers:                                                    │
│   Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**What you've accomplished:**
- ✓ Added multiple HTTP Request samplers
- ✓ Configured GET requests with parameters
- ✓ Configured POST requests with JSON body
- ✓ Set appropriate headers

**Listeners** capture and display test results. They're essential for understanding what happened during your test.

**Steps to add:**

```
1. Right-click on Thread Group
2. Add → Listener → [choose listener type]
```

**Essential Listeners for Beginners:**

**1. View Results Tree** (for debugging)
```
Purpose: See individual requests and responses

Shows:
- Request details (headers, body, cookies)
- Response data (HTML, JSON, etc.)
- Response time, size, status code
- Assertion results

Best for: Test development, debugging failures
⚠️ Warning: Memory intensive, not for large tests
```

**2. Summary Report** (for overview)
```
Purpose: Statistical summary of all requests

Columns:
- Label: sampler name
- # Samples: number of requests
- Average: average response time (ms)
- Min: minimum response time
- Max: maximum response time
- Std. Dev.: standard deviation
- Error %: percentage of failed requests
- Throughput: requests per second
- Received KB/sec: data received
- Sent KB/sec: data sent

Best for: Quick overview of test results
```

**3. Aggregate Report** (for detailed analysis)
```
Purpose: More detailed statistics with percentiles

Additional columns:
- Median: 50th percentile response time
- 90% Line: 90th percentile
- 95% Line: 95th percentile
- 99% Line: 99th percentile

Best for: Performance analysis, SLA validation
```

**4. Graph Results** (for visual trends)
```
Purpose: Visual representation of response times

Shows:
- Response time over time
- Average line
- Median line

Best for: Spotting performance degradation patterns
```

**5. Response Time Graph** (for trends)
```
Purpose: Detailed response time distribution

Shows:
- Response times over time
- Moving average
- Percentile lines

Best for: Detailed performance analysis
```

**Listener Best Practices:**

```
✅ DO:
- Use View Results Tree for debugging only
- Disable or remove listeners for actual load tests
- Save results to file for later analysis
- Use Simple Data Writer for large tests

❌ DON'T:
- Keep View Results Tree enabled during load tests
- Use too many listeners simultaneously
- Rely only on GUI for results (save to file)

For large tests:
- Disable all GUI listeners
- Use: jmeter -n -t test.jmx -l results.jtl
- Generate HTML report after test: -e -o report
```

**What you've accomplished:**
- ✓ Added multiple listeners
- ✓ Learned what each listener shows
- ✓ Understood best practices for listeners

steps.step: 6. Add Timers for Realistic Think Time
details:
**Timers** add pauses between requests to simulate real user behavior. Without timers, requests would fire as fast as possible – not realistic!

**Steps to add a Timer:**

```
1. Right-click on Thread Group
2. Add → Timer → [choose timer type]
```

**Common Timer Types:**

**1. Constant Timer** (simplest)
```
Purpose: Fixed delay between requests

Configuration:
  Thread Delay: 2000 milliseconds (2 seconds)

Effect: Each request waits exactly 2 seconds after previous

Use when: All users have same think time, predictable
```

**2. Uniform Random Timer** (more realistic)
```
Purpose: Random delay within a range

Configuration:
  Random Delay Maximum: 3000 milliseconds
  Constant Delay Offset: 1000 milliseconds

Result: Random delay between 1000-4000ms (1000 + 0-3000)

Use when: Users have varying think times
```

**3. Gaussian Random Timer** (most realistic)
```
Purpose: Normal distribution of delays (bell curve)

Configuration:
  Deviation: 1000 milliseconds
  Constant Delay Offset: 2000 milliseconds

Result: Most delays around 2000ms, some shorter/longer

Use when: Want statistically realistic user behavior
```

**4. Constant Throughput Timer** (for rate control)
```
Purpose: Control requests per minute

Configuration:
  Target Throughput: 60.0 (requests per minute)
  Calculate Throughput on: all threads

Use when: Need to maintain specific request rate
```

**Timer Placement Examples:**

```
Scenario: User browses products

Thread Group
├── HTTP Request - Homepage
├── ⏱️ Timer - Think 2-4 seconds
├── HTTP Request - Search
├── ⏱️ Timer - Think 1-3 seconds
├── HTTP Request - View Product
├── ⏱️ Timer - Think 3-5 seconds
└── HTTP Request - Add to Cart
```

**Timer Best Practices:**

```
✅ DO:
- Use timers to simulate realistic user behavior
- Place timers AFTER requests (delay before next action)
- Use random timers for more realistic scenarios
- Start with constant timers, then add randomness

❌ DON'T:
- Forget timers (tests will be unrealistically fast)
- Use zero delay (unless testing API limits)
- Put timer before first request (unnecessary delay)

Rule of thumb:
- Browsing: 2-5 seconds between clicks
- Form filling: 5-10 seconds
- API calls: 0-1 seconds
- Checkout process: 10-30 seconds
```

**What you've accomplished:**
- ✓ Added timers to simulate think time
- ✓ Learned different timer types
- ✓ Understood where to place timers
- ✓ Made test more realistic

**Assertions** validate that responses meet expectations. Without assertions, you might have successful HTTP calls that return error pages!

**Steps to add an Assertion:**

```
1. Right-click on a Sampler (or Thread Group for all)
2. Add → Assertions → [choose assertion type]
```

**Essential Assertion Types:**

**1. Response Assertion** (most common)
```
Purpose: Validate response codes, text, headers

Configuration for status code:
  Field to Test: Response Code
  Pattern Matching Rules: Equals
  Patterns to Test: 200

Configuration for response text:
  Field to Test: Text Response
  Pattern Matching Rules: Contains
  Patterns to Test: Welcome|Dashboard|Success

Configuration for error detection:
  Field to Test: Text Response
  Pattern Matching Rules: Not Contains
  Patterns to Test: Error|Exception|Fail
```

**2. Duration Assertion** (performance check)
```
Purpose: Ensure responses are fast enough

Configuration:
  Duration in milliseconds: 2000

Fails if response takes longer than 2 seconds
```

**3. Size Assertion** (data integrity)
```
Purpose: Validate response size

Configuration:
  Size in bytes: 1024
  Compare: Equals | Not Equals | Greater Than | Less Than

Use for: Checking if response has expected content
```

**4. JSON Assertion** (for API testing)
```
Purpose: Validate JSON responses

Configuration:
  JSON Path: $.data.user.id
  Expected Value: 12345
  Validate against expected value

Use for: API contract validation
```

**5. XPath Assertion** (for XML/SOAP)
```
Purpose: Validate XML/SOAP responses

Configuration:
  XPath: //response/status
  Expected Value: success

Use for: Legacy XML APIs
```

**6. HTML Assertion** (for web pages)
```
Purpose: Validate HTML structure

Use for: Checking if page title is correct
```

**Assertion Placement Examples:**

```
Option 1: Attach to specific sampler
HTTP Request - Login
├── ✅ Response Assertion (code = 200)
├── ✅ JSON Assertion (token exists)
└── ✅ Duration Assertion (< 3 sec)

Option 2: Attach to Thread Group (applies to all)
Thread Group
├── ✅ Duration Assertion (< 5 sec) // applies to all requests
├── HTTP Request - Homepage
├── HTTP Request - Search
└── HTTP Request - Product
```

**Assertion Best Practices:**

```
✅ DO:
- Always add assertions to validate success
- Check status codes (200, 201, etc.)
- Validate key content exists
- Set duration thresholds for performance
- Add negative assertions (check for errors)

❌ DON'T:
- Assume 200 means success (could be error page!)
- Ignore error responses (they're failures!)
- Set duration thresholds too low (false failures)
- Over-assert (test can become brittle)

Good assertion suite includes:
✓ Status code is correct
✓ Expected content exists
✓ Response time is acceptable
✓ No error messages present
```

**What you've accomplished:**
- ✓ Added assertions to validate responses
- ✓ Learned different assertion types
- ✓ Understood where to place assertions
- ✓ Made test validate correctness, not just speed

=========================================================================

=========================================================================

Test Plan: E-Commerce Performance Test
Description: Simulates realistic user behavior on an e-commerce site
Author: Performance Team
Created: 2025-02-20

=========================================================================
TEST PLAN STRUCTURE
=========================================================================

📋 E-Commerce Performance Test
│
├── User Defined Variables
│   ├── HOST = api.example.com
│   ├── PROTOCOL = https

│   │   └── Server: ${HOST}, Protocol: ${PROTOCOL}
│   ├── 📁 Create Test Users
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Create User 1
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Create User 2
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Create User 3
│   │   └── ✅ Response Assertion (201)
│   └── 📁 Create Test Products
│       ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Create Product A
│       ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Create Product B
│       └── ✅ Response Assertion (201)
│
├── 📁 Main Traffic Simulation (100 users, 60 sec ramp-up, 3 loops)
│   ├── 🎛️ HTTP Request Defaults
│   │   └── Server: ${HOST}, Protocol: ${PROTOCOL}
│   │
│   ├── 📁 User Journey 1: Browse Products
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Homepage
│   │   ├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (2000-5000ms)
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Search "laptop"
│   │   ├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (2000-5000ms)
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - View Product Details
│   │   ├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (3000-7000ms)
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Add to Cart
│   │   └── ✅ Response Assertion (200)
│   │
│   ├── 📁 User Journey 2: Checkout Process
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - View Cart
│   │   ├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (2000-4000ms)
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Login
│   │   │   ├── 🎛️ HTTP Header Manager (JSON)
│   │   │   ├── 🎛️ Body Data (JSON)
│   │   │   ├── ✅ Response Assertion (200)
│   │   │   ├── ✅ JSON Assertion (token exists)
│   │   │   └── 🔧 Regular Expression Extractor (save token)
│   │   ├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (2000-4000ms)
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Add Shipping Address
│   │   ├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (3000-6000ms)
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Select Payment
│   │   ├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (4000-8000ms)
│   │   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Place Order
│   │   └── ✅ Response Assertion (201)
│   │
│   └── 📁 Assertions (Global)
│       ├── ✅ Duration Assertion (< 5000ms) for all requests
│       └── ✅ Response Assertion (not contains "error")
│
├── 📁 Teardown Thread Group (Clean up)
│   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Delete Test Users
│   ├── ✅ Response Assertion (200)
│   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Delete Test Products
│   └── ✅ Response Assertion (200)
│
└── 📁 Listeners
    ├── 👂 View Results Tree (for debugging, disabled for load test)
    ├── 👂 Summary Report
    ├── 👂 Aggregate Report
    └── 👂 Response Time Graph

=========================================================================
TEST CONFIGURATION SUMMARY
=========================================================================

Thread Group: Main Traffic Simulation
├── Number of Threads: 100
├── Ramp-up: 60 seconds
├── Loop Count: 3
└── Total Requests: 100 × 3 × 7 ≈ 2,100 requests

Think Times:
├── Between actions: 2-8 seconds (user dependent)
├── Total user session: 30-60 seconds
└── Realistic user behavior

Assertions:
├── Status codes (200, 201)
├── Response time < 5 seconds
├── JSON structure validation
└── No error messages

=========================================================================
EXPECTED RESULTS
=========================================================================

Successful test indicators:
✓ All status codes 200/201
✓ Response times < 5 seconds
✓ No error messages
✓ Throughput appropriate for 100 users
✓ All assertions pass

Performance benchmarks:
├── Average response time: < 2 seconds
├── 95th percentile: < 4 seconds
├── Error rate: < 1%
└── Throughput: 10-20 requests/second

=========================================================================
HOW TO RUN THIS TEST
=========================================================================

1. Save test plan as ecommerce-test.jmx

2. For debugging (GUI mode, small scale):
   - Set threads to 2-5
   - Enable View Results Tree
   - Run and check each request

3. For actual load test (CLI mode):
   - Disable View Results Tree
   - Run: 
     jmeter -n -t ecommerce-test.jmx -l results.jtl
   - Generate report:
     jmeter -g results.jtl -o report -e

4. For distributed testing:
   jmeter -n -t ecommerce-test.jmx -l results.jtl \
          -R slave1,slave2,slave3

=========================================================================
INTERPRETING RESULTS
=========================================================================

Look for these indicators in Summary Report:

✅ Good:
- Error % < 1%
- Throughput stable
- Average response time consistent
- No samples with extreme values

⚠️ Warning:
- Error % 1-5%
- Increasing response times
- Throughput decreasing
- High standard deviation

❌ Problem:
- Error % > 5%
- Response times > 5 seconds
- Throughput dropping to zero
- OutOfMemory errors

=========================================================================
TROUBLESHOOTING TIPS
=========================================================================

If tests fail:
1. Check assertions – maybe thresholds too strict?
2. Verify test data exists
3. Check server logs
4. Increase think times
5. Reduce load gradually
6. Check JMeter memory settings

=========================================================================
"A well-designed test plan is worth a thousand results."
=========================================================================
```

content.title: Test Plan Best Practices
content.explanation:
**Proven Strategies for Effective JMeter Test Plans:**

**1. Test Plan Organization**

```
✅ DO:
- Use descriptive names for all elements
- Group related requests using controllers
- Add comments explaining test purpose
- Use Setup/Teardown thread groups
- Keep test plans modular and reusable
- Version control your .jmx files

❌ DON'T:
- Leave default names ("HTTP Request")
- Mix different test scenarios in one thread group
- Forget to document test plan
- Create monolithic, unorganized test plans
```

**2. Data-Driven Testing**

```
Use CSV Data Set Config for test data:

1. Create data.csv:
   username,password,product
   user1,pass1,laptop
   user2,pass2,phone
   user3,pass3,tablet

2. Add CSV Data Set Config:
   - Filename: data.csv
   - Variable Names: username,password,product
   - Delimiter: ,
   - Recycle on EOF: True

3. Use variables in requests:
   - /api/login?user=${username}&pass=${password}
   - /api/search?q=${product}

Benefits: Same test runs with multiple data sets!
```

**3. Correlation (Dynamic Values)**

```
Many applications return dynamic values (session IDs, tokens).

Use Regular Expression Extractor:

1. Add as child of request that returns dynamic value
2. Configure:
   - Reference Name: sessionId
   - Regular Expression: "sessionId":"([^"]+)"
   - Template: $1$
   - Match No.: 1

3. Use in subsequent requests:
   - Header: X-Session: ${sessionId}
   - URL: /api/data?sid=${sessionId}
```

**4. Think Time Realism**

```
Make think times realistic:

├── Browsing: 2-5 seconds
├── Reading content: 5-15 seconds
├── Form filling: 5-10 seconds
├── Checkout: 10-30 seconds
├── API calls: 0-1 seconds

Use random timers for variety:
- Uniform Random Timer (min, max)
- Gaussian Random Timer (normal distribution)
```

**5. Assertion Strategy**

```
Always validate responses:

Critical assertions (always include):
├── Status code (200, 201, etc.)
├── Response time (< threshold)
├── No error messages

Business assertions (scenario-dependent):
├── JSON path contains expected value
├── Page title is correct
├── Total amount matches calculation

Performance assertions:
├── Duration < SLA threshold
├── Throughput > minimum
```

**6. Test Data Management**

```
Use separate data sets for:
├── Development (small, varied)
├── Staging (production-like)
├── Production (realistic, masked)

Create test data in Setup thread group
Clean up in Teardown thread group
Use unique data to avoid conflicts
```

**7. Error Handling**

```
Configure error handling in Thread Group:

Action after error:
├── Continue – log error and proceed (recommended for analysis)
├── Stop Thread – stop current virtual user
├── Stop Test – abort entire test
├── Stop Test Now – immediate abort

For load tests, usually choose "Continue" to see all errors.
```

**8. Test Plan Checklist**

```
□ PRE-TEST
   □ Test plan has descriptive name
   □ Comments explain purpose
   □ Variables defined for config
   □ Test data prepared
   □ Assertions added for validation
   □ Timers added for realism
   □ Error handling configured

□ DURING TEST
   □ Listeners disabled for load test
   □ Results saved to file
   □ Server resources monitored
   □ JMeter memory adequate

□ POST-TEST
   □ Results analyzed
   □ Reports generated
   □ Findings documented
   □ Test plan versioned
```

**9. Common Mistakes to Avoid**

```
❌ MISTAKES

1. No assertions – can't tell if test actually passed
2. No timers – unrealistic load, server may be overwhelmed
3. Hardcoded values – test breaks when data changes
4. Too many listeners – slows down test, affects results
5. Not saving results – can't analyze later
6. Running large tests in GUI – memory issues, inaccurate results
7. Ignoring errors – failures hide behind successful HTTP codes
8. One-size-fits-all think times – not realistic
```

**10. Performance Testing Principles**

```
📊 KEY PRINCIPLES

1. Test Early, Test Often
   - Performance testing isn't just for the end
   - Find issues when they're cheap to fix

2. Environment Matters
   - Test in environment similar to production
   - Account for network latency, hardware differences

3. Repeatability
   - Same test should give same results
   - Control variables (data, time, environment)

4. Isolation
   - Test one thing at a time
   - Understand what's causing issues

5. Realism
   - Simulate real user behavior
   - Realistic think times, user flows
   - Realistic data volumes

6. Measurement
   - Define success criteria before testing
   - Measure what matters (response time, throughput, errors)
   - Understand percentiles, not just averages
```

**Remember:** A well-designed test plan is the foundation of meaningful performance testing. Take time to design it right, and your results will be reliable and actionable.
```

content.title: Understanding JMeter Thread Groups
content.explanation:
**The Foundation of User Simulation:**

**1. What is a Thread Group?**

A Thread Group is the starting point of any JMeter test plan. It controls the number of virtual users (threads) that will execute your test script. Each thread represents a real user interacting with your application.

```
THREAD GROUP = Virtual User Pool

Each thread = One virtual user
Threads run in parallel = Concurrent users

Example:
Thread Group with 100 threads = 100 concurrent virtual users
```

**2. Why Thread Groups Matter**

```
Thread Groups determine:
├── How many users (load level)
├── How fast users arrive (ramp-up)
├── How long they stay (duration)
├── How many actions they perform (loops)
└── When they run (schedule)

They are the heart of your load test configuration!
```

**3. Anatomy of a Thread Group**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Thread Group                                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Name: [Descriptive name]                                    │
│ Comments: [Purpose of this group]                           │
│                                                             │
│ Action to be taken after a Sampler error:                   │
│ ○ Continue  ○ Stop Thread  ○ Stop Test  ○ Stop Test Now    │
│                                                             │
│ Thread Properties:                                          │
│   Number of Threads (users): _____                         │
│   Ramp-up period (seconds): _____                           │
│   Loop Count: _____  [ ] Infinite                           │
│                                                             │
│ [ ] Same user on each iteration                             │
│ [ ] Delay thread creation until needed                      │
│ [ ] Specify thread lifetime                                 │
│     ├── Duration (seconds): _____                           │
│     └── Startup delay (seconds): _____                      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**4. Key Thread Group Concepts**

| Concept | Description | Example |
|---------|-------------|---------|
| **Thread** | A single virtual user | 1 thread = 1 simulated user |
| **Ramp-up** | Time to start all threads | 100 threads in 60 seconds |
| **Loop** | Number of test repetitions | Each user repeats test 5 times |
| **Iteration** | One complete pass through samplers | User completes one shopping trip |
| **Scheduler** | Time-based test control | Run test for 1 hour |

**5. Thread Group Types**

```
📁 THREE TYPES OF THREAD GROUPS
────────────────────────────────

1. Setup Thread Group
   ├── Runs BEFORE main test
   ├── Usually 1 thread, 1 iteration
   ├── Purpose: Create test data, log in, prepare environment
   └── Example: Create 100 test users for the main test

2. Thread Group (Main)
   ├── Runs the actual load test
   ├── Multiple threads, loops
   ├── Purpose: Simulate real users
   └── Example: 100 users browsing and buying

3. Teardown Thread Group
   ├── Runs AFTER main test
   ├── Usually 1 thread, 1 iteration
   ├── Purpose: Clean up test data, log out
   └── Example: Delete test users created in setup
```

**6. How Threads Execute**

```
Execution flow:

1. JMeter starts Thread Group
2. Creates threads according to ramp-up schedule
3. Each thread executes samplers in order
4. Threads pause for timers (think time)
5. After completing all samplers, thread loops (if loop count > 1)
6. After completing all loops, thread stops
7. Process repeats for all threads

Visual representation:

Time 0s:    Thread 1 starts
Time 1s:    Thread 2 starts
Time 2s:    Thread 3 starts
...
Time 59s:   Thread 100 starts

All 100 threads active from 60s onward
```

**7. Simple Example**

```
Thread Group: Website Browsers
├── Number of Threads: 50
├── Ramp-up: 30 seconds
├── Loop Count: 10
└── Samplers: 5 requests per loop

Total requests = 50 threads × 10 loops × 5 requests = 2,500 requests

Load pattern:
- Users arrive: 1-2 per second
- Peak load (all 50 active): after 30 seconds
- Test duration: approx 30 sec ramp-up + (10 loops × execution time)
```

**8. When to Use Multiple Thread Groups**

```
Single Thread Group: Simple tests, one user type

Multiple Thread Groups: Complex scenarios

Example E-commerce test:
├── 📁 Setup: Create test products (1 user)
├── 📁 Browsers: 70 users browsing products
├── 📁 Buyers: 20 users making purchases
├── 📁 Checkout: 10 users completing checkout
└── 📁 Teardown: Clean up test data (1 user)

Benefits:
- Different user behaviors
- Different loads per user type
- Setup/teardown isolated
- Clearer test organization
```

**9. Thread Group Best Practices**

```
✅ DO:
- Give meaningful names ("Homepage Browsers" not "Thread Group")
- Use Setup/Teardown for initialization/cleanup
- Start with small thread counts, then increase
- Calculate expected total requests
- Monitor actual vs expected thread count
- Use scheduling for time-based tests

❌ DON'T:
- Use infinite loops without scheduling (test never ends)
- Mix different user behaviors in one group
- Forget about ramp-up (all users starting at once = spike)
- Use too many threads for machine capacity
- Ignore thread group ordering (Setup → Main → Teardown)
```
```

details:
**Adding a Thread Group:**

```
1. Right-click on Test Plan
2. Add → Threads (Users) → Thread Group
3. The new thread group appears in the tree
4. Select it to configure in right panel
```

**Naming Convention:**

```
Good names: "Homepage Users", "Checkout Flow", "API Browsers"
Bad names: "Thread Group", "Users", "Test1"

Format: [Purpose] - [Details]
Examples:
- Browsers - 100 users
- Buyers - 20 users, 5 loops
- Setup - Create Test Data
```

**Thread Group Properties Overview:**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Thread Group: Browsers - 100 users                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Comments: Simulates regular website visitors                │
│                                                             │
│ Action after error: Continue                                 │
│                                                             │
│ Number of Threads: 100                                      │
│ Ramp-up period: 60                                          │
│ Loop Count: 5                                               │
│ [ ] Infinite                                                │
│                                                             │
│ [ ] Same user on each iteration                              │
│ [✓] Delay thread creation until needed                      │
│ [ ] Specify thread lifetime                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**What you've done:**
- ✓ Added a thread group
- ✓ Given it a meaningful name
- ✓ Ready to configure specific settings

steps.action: Set the number of virtual users
details:
**Number of Threads = Number of concurrent virtual users**

**How to decide thread count:**

```
Based on your performance goals:
├── Average load: Expected concurrent users
├── Peak load: Maximum expected users
├── Stress test: Gradually increase until failure
└── Soak test: Moderate load over long period

Common starting points:
├── Smoke test: 1-5 threads
├── Load test: 50-500 threads
├── Stress test: 500-5000+ threads
└── Endurance test: 100-500 threads over hours
```

**Configuration examples:**

```
Scenario A: Normal business hours
├── Expected concurrent users: 200
├── Number of Threads: 200
├── Ramp-up: 120 seconds (2 minutes)
└── Loop Count: 10 (or use scheduler for duration)

Scenario B: Stress test to find breaking point
├── Number of Threads: Start at 100, increase
├── Use multiple thread groups or iterations
├── Monitor when errors occur
└── Find maximum capacity

Scenario C: Smoke test (quick sanity check)
├── Number of Threads: 2
├── Ramp-up: 2 seconds
├── Loop Count: 1
└── Verify basic functionality
```

**Important considerations:**

```
⚠️ Physical limits:
- Each thread consumes memory
- 1000 threads ≈ 1 GB RAM
- Your machine has limits
- Consider distributed testing for >1000 users

⚠️ Application limits:
- Server may have connection limits
- Database connection pools
- Thread pools in app server
- Don't exceed real-world limits
```

**Using variables for thread count:**

```
Define at Test Plan level:
User Defined Variables:
├── USERS = 100
├── RAMPUP = 60
└── LOOPS = 5

In Thread Group:
├── Number of Threads: ${USERS}
├── Ramp-up: ${RAMPUP}
└── Loop Count: ${LOOPS}

Benefits: Easy to change all at once!
```

**What you've learned:**
- ✓ How to choose thread count
- ✓ Relationship between threads and load
- ✓ Physical limitations to consider
- ✓ Using variables for flexibility

**Ramp-up = Time to start all threads**

**Why ramp-up matters:**

```
Without ramp-up (0 seconds):
- All 100 users start at exactly the same moment
- Creates a massive spike in load
- Not realistic for most applications
- Can overwhelm server unnecessarily

With ramp-up (60 seconds):
- Users start gradually over 60 seconds
- Load increases smoothly
- More realistic (users arrive over time)
- Gentler on server
```

**How ramp-up works:**

```
Formula: Users per second = Threads / Ramp-up

Examples:
100 users / 10 seconds = 10 users/second
100 users / 100 seconds = 1 user/second
100 users / 1 second = 100 users/second (spike)

Rule of thumb: Start with ramp-up = threads
Example: 100 threads → 60-100 seconds ramp-up
```

**Ramp-up strategies by test type:**

```
📊 SMOKE TEST (quick check)
   Threads: 5
   Ramp-up: 5 seconds
   Rate: 1 user/second

📈 LOAD TEST (normal conditions)
   Threads: 200
   Ramp-up: 120 seconds
   Rate: 1.67 users/second

📊 STRESS TEST (find limits)
   Threads: 1000
   Ramp-up: 300 seconds (5 minutes)
   Rate: 3.33 users/second
   Then hold, then increase

📉 SPIKE TEST (sudden surge)
   Threads: 500
   Ramp-up: 5 seconds
   Rate: 100 users/second
   Tests handling of sudden traffic
```

**Ramp-up patterns:**

```
Linear ramp-up (default):
Users start at constant rate
Good for most tests

Step ramp-up (using multiple thread groups):
Group1: 100 users, ramp-up 60s
Group2: 200 users, ramp-up 60s (starts after group1)
Group3: 300 users, ramp-up 60s
Creates stepped load pattern

Delayed start:
Use scheduler to start thread group at specific time
```

**Ramp-up best practices:**

```
✅ DO:
- Make ramp-up at least as long as thread count
- Watch server metrics during ramp-up
- Adjust based on real user behavior
- Consider time of day patterns

❌ DON'T:
- Use 0 ramp-up for load tests (creates spike)
- Make ramp-up too short for large thread counts
- Ignore ramp-up in test analysis

Formula to calculate when full load reached:
Full load time = ramp-up + (loop count × iteration time)
```

**What you've learned:**
- ✓ Purpose of ramp-up
- ✓ How to calculate arrival rate
- ✓ Different ramp-up strategies
- ✓ Relationship with thread count

steps.action: Set how many times users repeat actions
details:
**Loop Count = Number of times each thread repeats the test**

**Understanding loops:**

```
Each thread executes all samplers in the thread group.
After finishing, it starts again from the beginning.

Thread with 5 loops:
Loop 1: Homepage → Search → Product → Cart
Loop 2: Homepage → Search → Product → Cart
Loop 3: Homepage → Search → Product → Cart
Loop 4: Homepage → Search → Product → Cart
Loop 5: Homepage → Search → Product → Cart
Then thread stops
```

**Loop count strategies:**

```
Scenario A: Fixed number of actions
├── Threads: 100
├── Loops: 10
├── Samplers: 5 per loop
├── Total requests: 100 × 10 × 5 = 5,000
└── Predictable total, good for planning

Scenario B: Infinite loops with duration
├── Threads: 100
├── Loop Count: Infinite
├── Scheduler: Duration 3600 seconds (1 hour)
├── Total requests: Depends on response times
└── Good for endurance testing

Scenario C: Single iteration
├── Threads: 100
├── Loops: 1
├── Each user does one complete journey
└── Good for smoke tests, setup/teardown
```

**Loop count vs Duration:**

```
Use loop count when:
- You need exact number of iterations
- Test has natural completion point
- Comparing results across runs

Use duration when:
- Testing for specific time period
- Real users have variable session lengths
- Doing endurance/soak testing

You can use both:
- Loop count with scheduler duration
- Threads stop when either condition met
```

**Calculating total requests:**

```
Total Requests = Threads × Loops × Samplers per Loop

Example: 100 threads, 5 loops, 8 samplers
Total = 100 × 5 × 8 = 4,000 requests

With think times, test duration =
(loops × (samplers × think time + response time)) + ramp-up
```

**Loop count examples by scenario:**

```
📋 E-commerce browsing:
   Loops: 3-5 (users browse multiple items)
   Each loop: Home → Search → View → Cart

📋 API testing:
   Loops: 10-100 (repeat same API calls)
   Each loop: Single API request

📋 User session:
   Loops: 1 (one complete journey)
   But journey has many steps

📋 Endurance test:
   Loops: Infinite
   Duration: 8 hours
```

**What you've learned:**
- ✓ How loops work
- ✓ When to use fixed loops vs infinite
- ✓ How to calculate total requests
- ✓ Relationship between loops and test duration

steps.action: Decide what happens when requests fail
details:
**Action after Sampler error** controls test behavior when a request fails.

**Four options:**

```
1. Continue (Recommended for most tests)
   ├── Log error and continue with next samplers
   ├── Best for: Seeing all errors, analyzing failure patterns
   ├── Test continues even with failures
   └── Use for: Load tests, analysis

2. Stop Thread
   ├── Stop current virtual user only
   ├── Other threads continue
   ├── Best for: When one user's failure shouldn't affect others
   └── Use for: Scenarios where users can fail independently

3. Stop Test
   ├── Stop all threads gracefully
   ├── Complete current iterations
   ├── Best for: When any failure invalidates the test
   └── Use for: Critical path testing

4. Stop Test Now
   ├── Immediate stop of all threads
   ├── No waiting for iterations to complete
   ├── Best for: Emergency stop, catastrophic failures
   └── Use for: When test environment is broken
```

**Choosing the right option:**

```
Load Testing:     Continue (see all errors)
Functional Test:  Stop Test (first failure fails test)
Smoke Test:       Stop Thread (isolate issues)
Debugging:        Continue (see all problems)
CI/CD Pipeline:   Stop Test (fail fast)
```

**Impact on test results:**

```
Continue:
- Complete test, full picture of failures
- May have many errors

Stop Thread:
- Missing data from stopped threads
- Harder to calculate total capacity

Stop Test:
- Test ends early
- May miss later performance issues
- Wasted test time
```

**What you've learned:**
- ✓ Four error handling options
- ✓ When to use each
- ✓ Impact on test results

**Advanced Thread Group options:**

**1. Same user on each iteration**

```
What it does: Preserves HTTP state between iterations
- Cookies are maintained
- Cache is maintained
- Session continues

When to use:
- Simulating returning users
- Testing sessions that span multiple visits
- When login happens once, then multiple actions

When not to use:
- Testing new users each time
- Anonymous browsing
- API testing without sessions
```

**2. Delay thread creation until needed**

```
What it does: Creates threads during ramp-up instead of all at once

Benefits:
- Saves memory during ramp-up
- More efficient resource usage
- Recommended to keep enabled

When to disable:
- Very rare, almost always keep checked
```

**3. Specify thread lifetime (Scheduler)**

```
Enables time-based test control:

Duration: How long the test runs
- Format: seconds
- Example: 3600 (1 hour)
- Test stops after this time

Startup delay: When to start
- Format: seconds
- Example: 60 (start after 1 minute)
- Useful for coordinating multiple thread groups

Configuration examples:

Example 1: Run for exactly 30 minutes
├── Duration: 1800
├── Loop: Infinite
└── Test stops after 30 minutes

Example 2: Start after other groups
├── Startup delay: 120
├── Duration: 600
└── Starts 2 minutes after test begins, runs 10 minutes

Example 3: Fixed time with loops
├── Loop: 100
├── Duration: 3600
└── Stops after 1 hour OR 100 loops, whichever comes first
```

**Scheduler use cases:**

```
📊 Endurance Testing
   ├── Duration: 28800 (8 hours)
   ├── Loop: Infinite
   └── Tests system stability over time

📈 Staggered Load
   ├── Group1: No delay, duration 300
   ├── Group2: Delay 300, duration 300
   ├── Group3: Delay 600, duration 300
   └── Creates increasing load pattern

📉 Peak Hour Simulation
   ├── Delay: 3600 (start after 1 hour of baseline)
   ├── Duration: 3600 (run for 1 hour)
   └── Simulates lunch hour traffic
```

**What you've learned:**
- ✓ Same user option for sessions
- ✓ Delay thread creation (always keep)
- ✓ Scheduler for time-based tests
- ✓ Complex test scenarios

content.title: Setup, Main, and Teardown Thread Groups
content.explanation:
**The Complete Test Lifecycle:**

**1. Setup Thread Group**

```
Purpose: Prepare the test environment
Timing: Runs ONCE before all main thread groups

Typical uses:
├── Create test data (users, products, orders)
├── Authenticate and get tokens
├── Warm up caches
├── Verify environment is ready
└── Initialize counters

Configuration:
├── Threads: Usually 1
├── Loops: 1
├── Ramp-up: 0 or 1
└── No need for many users
```

**Setup Thread Group Example:**

```
📁 Setup Thread Group - Create Test Data
├── Number of Threads: 1
├── Loop Count: 1
├── Ramp-up: 1
│
├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Admin Login
│   └── ✅ Assertion (200)
│
├── 🔧 Regular Expression Extractor - Get Token
│
├── 📁 Create 100 Test Users
│   ├── 🎛️ CSV Data Set Config (user_data.csv)
│   ├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Create User
│   ├── ⏱️ Constant Timer (100ms) - avoid rate limiting
│   └── ✅ Assertion (201)
│
└── 🎯 HTTP Request - Create Products
    └── ✅ Assertion (201)
```

**2. Main Thread Groups**

```
Purpose: Simulate real user load
Timing: Run after setup, possibly in parallel

Types of main thread groups:
├── Browsers - Users just looking
├── Buyers - Users making purchases
├── API Consumers - Programmatic access
├── Admin Users - Backend operations
└── Mixed - Multiple user types
```

**Main Thread Group Example - Multiple User Types:**

```
📁 Browsers - 70 users (70% of traffic)
├── Threads: 70
├── Ramp-up: 60
├── Loops: 5
├── Think time: 2-5 seconds
└── Actions: Browse products, view details

📁 Buyers - 20 users (20% of traffic)
├── Threads: 20
├── Ramp-up: 60
├── Loops: 3
├── Think time: 3-8 seconds
└── Actions: Search, view, add to cart

📁 Checkout Users - 10 users (10% of traffic)
├── Threads: 10
├── Ramp-up: 60
├── Loops: 2
├── Think time: 5-15 seconds
└── Actions: Full checkout process
```

**3. Teardown Thread Group**

```
Purpose: Clean up after the test
Timing: Runs ONCE after all main thread groups complete

Typical uses:
├── Delete test data created in setup
├── Logout users
├── Reset system state
├── Collect final metrics
└── Send notifications

Configuration:
├── Threads: Usually 1
├── Loops: 1
├── Ramp-up: 0 or 1
└── Ensure it runs even if test fails (use tearDownOnShutdown)
```

**Teardown Thread Group Example:**

```
📁 Teardown Thread Group - Clean Up
├── Number of Threads: 1
├── Loop Count: 1
├── Ramp-up: 1
│
├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Delete Test Users
│   └── ✅ Assertion (200/204)
│
├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Delete Test Products
│   └── ✅ Assertion (200/204)
│
├── 🎯 HTTP Request - Logout
│
└── 🎯 HTTP Request - Send Test Completion Notification
```

**4. Execution Order**

```
Time Line:
───┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┬─────►
   │                  │                  │
   ▼                  ▼                  ▼
Setup TG        Main TGs (parallel)   Teardown TG

If "Run Thread Groups consecutively" is checked:
   Setup → Group1 → Group2 → Group3 → Teardown

If unchecked (default):
   Setup → (Group1, Group2, Group3 in parallel) → Teardown
```

**5. Complete Example with All Three**

```
📋 E-Commerce Load Test
│
├── 📁 Setup Thread Group
│   ├── 🎯 Admin Login
│   ├── 🔧 Extract Token
│   ├── 🎯 Create 100 Test Users
│   └── 🎯 Create 50 Test Products
│
├── 📁 Browsers (70 users)
│   ├── 🎯 Homepage
│   ├── ⏱️ Think 2s
│   ├── 🎯 Search
│   ├── ⏱️ Think 3s
│   ├── 🎯 View Product
│   └── ⏱️ Think 4s
│
├── 📁 Buyers (20 users)
│   ├── 🎯 Login (using test users)
│   ├── 🔧 Extract Session
│   ├── 🎯 Browse Categories
│   ├── 🎯 Add to Cart
│   └── 🎯 View Cart
│
├── 📁 Checkout Users (10 users)
│   ├── 🎯 Login
│   ├── 🎯 Add to Cart
│   ├── 🎯 Checkout
│   ├── 🎯 Enter Payment
│   └── 🎯 Confirm Order
│
└── 📁 Teardown Thread Group
    ├── 🎯 Delete Test Users
    └── 🎯 Delete Test Products
```

**6. Best Practices for Multiple Thread Groups**

```
✅ DO:
- Use Setup for data creation (single thread)
- Use Teardown for cleanup (single thread)
- Group similar user behaviors together
- Name groups clearly ("Browsers - 70%")
- Consider execution order (consecutive vs parallel)
- Ensure Setup succeeds before main test runs
- Make Teardown robust (should run even if test fails)

❌ DON'T:
- Put data creation in main thread groups (creates conflicts)
- Forget cleanup (leaves garbage data)
- Mix incompatible behaviors in one group
- Make Teardown dependent on test success
- Overwhelm server with too many groups starting at once
```

**7. Special Consideration: setUp Thread Group**

```
⚠️ Important Notes:

- If setUp fails, main thread groups may not run
- setUp runs with highest priority
- setUp is NOT affected by scheduler settings
- setUp runs even if test is stopped?

Teardown:
- Runs even if test is stopped manually
- Runs if setUp fails (configurable)
- Use for critical cleanup regardless of test outcome
```
```

content.title: E-Commerce Website User Simulation
content.scenario: Simulating different types of users on an e-commerce site
content.outcome: Realistic load patterns with multiple user behaviors
content.details:
```
=========================================================================
           E-COMMERCE WEBSITE - REALISTIC USER SIMULATION
=========================================================================

OVERVIEW
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
This test simulates a typical e-commerce website with multiple user types,
realistic think times, and varying traffic patterns throughout the day.

USER DISTRIBUTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Total target load: 1000 concurrent users

User Type Distribution:
├── New Visitors (40%): 400 users - First time visitors, browsing
├── Returning Shoppers (35%): 350 users - Know the site, comparison shop
├── Buyers (20%): 200 users - Intent to purchase
└── Checkout (5%): 50 users - Completing purchases

=========================================================================
SETUP THREAD GROUP - Test Data Preparation
=========================================================================

📁 Setup Thread Group
├── Number of Threads: 1
├── Ramp-up: 1
├── Loop Count: 1
└── Comments: Create test users and products

Test Data Requirements:
├── 1000 test user accounts (email/password combos)
├── 500 test products across categories
├── Inventory counts for each product
└── Promotional codes

Samplers:
├── 🎯 Admin Login
├── 🔧 Extract Auth Token
├── 📁 Loop Controller - Create 1000 Users
│   ├── 🎛️ CSV Data Set Config (user_data.csv)
│   ├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/users
│   ├── ✅ Response Assertion (201)
│   └── ⏱️ Constant Timer (100ms) - rate limiting
├── 📁 Loop Controller - Create 500 Products
│   ├── 🎛️ CSV Data Set Config (product_data.csv)
│   ├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/products
│   ├── ✅ Response Assertion (201)
│   └── ⏱️ Constant Timer (200ms)
└── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/inventory/initialize

=========================================================================
THREAD GROUP 1 - NEW VISITORS (400 users, 40% of traffic)
=========================================================================

📁 New Visitors
├── Number of Threads: 400
├── Ramp-up: 120 seconds (3.3 users/second)
├── Loop Count: 3 (each visitor views 3-4 pages)
├── Same user on each iteration: False (new session each time)
└── Comments: First-time visitors, browsing only

User Behavior Pattern:
```
User Journey:
1. Land on homepage (2-5 sec)
2. Search for product (3-8 sec)
3. View product details (5-15 sec)
4. Maybe another search (3-8 sec)
5. Leave without purchasing
```

Samplers:
├── 🎯 HTTP GET / - Homepage
│   └── ✅ Duration Assertion (< 3000ms)
├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (2000-5000ms) - Browse homepage
├── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/search?q=laptop&category=electronics
│   └── ✅ Response Assertion (contains "results")
├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (3000-8000ms) - Review results
├── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/products/${randomProductId}
│   └── ✅ Response Assertion (200)
├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (5000-15000ms) - Read details
├── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/search?q=${randomTerm}
│   └── ✅ Response Assertion (200)
└── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (3000-8000ms) - Before leaving

=========================================================================
THREAD GROUP 2 - RETURNING SHOPPERS (350 users, 35% of traffic)
=========================================================================

📁 Returning Shoppers
├── Number of Threads: 350
├── Ramp-up: 120 seconds (2.9 users/second)
├── Loop Count: 4
├── Same user on each iteration: True (maintain session)
└── Comments: Registered users, logged in, comparing products

User Behavior Pattern:
```
1. Login (10-20 sec)
2. Browse wishlist (5-10 sec)
3. Search and compare (10-20 sec)
4. View multiple products (5-15 sec each)
5. Add to wishlist or cart
6. May logout
```

Samplers:
├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/auth/login
│   ├── Body: {"email":"${testEmail}","password":"${testPass}"}
│   ├── ✅ Response Assertion (200)
│   └── 🔧 JSON Extractor - Extract session token
├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (10000-20000ms) - Typing credentials
├── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/user/wishlist
│   └── ✅ Response Assertion (200)
├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (5000-10000ms) - Review wishlist
├── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/search?q=${product1}&compare=true
├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (5000-10000ms) - Compare
├── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/search?q=${product2}&compare=true
├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (5000-10000ms) - Compare
├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/cart/add - 30% probability
│   └── Body: {"productId":${pid},"quantity":1}
├── ⏱️ Uniform Random Timer (3000-7000ms)
└── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/auth/logout - 20% probability

=========================================================================
THREAD GROUP 3 - BUYERS (200 users, 20% of traffic)
=========================================================================

📁 Buyers
├── Number of Threads: 200
├── Ramp-up: 120 seconds (1.7 users/second)
├── Loop Count: 2
├── Same user on each iteration: True
└── Comments: Users with intent to purchase

User Behavior Pattern:
```
1. Login
2. Search for specific product
3. Add to cart
4. Continue shopping
5. Add another item
6. Proceed to checkout
```

Samplers:
├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/auth/login
│   └── ✅ Assertions
├── ⏱️ Timer
├── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/search?q=${targetProduct}
├── ⏱️ Timer
├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/cart/add (first item)
├── ⏱️ Timer
├── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/cart
├── ⏱️ Timer
├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/cart/add (second item)
├── ⏱️ Timer
├── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/checkout/start
└── (continues to checkout thread)

=========================================================================
THREAD GROUP 4 - CHECKOUT (50 users, 5% of traffic)
=========================================================================

📁 Checkout
├── Number of Threads: 50
├── Ramp-up: 60 seconds (0.8 users/second)
├── Loop Count: 1 (one purchase per session)
└── Comments: Completing purchases

User Behavior Pattern:
```
1. Login (if not already)
2. Review cart
3. Enter shipping info (10-30 sec)
4. Enter payment info (15-30 sec)
5. Review order (10-20 sec)
6. Place order
7. View confirmation
```

Samplers:
├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/auth/login
├── ⏱️ Timer (10000-30000ms)
├── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/cart/review
├── ⏱️ Timer (5000-10000ms)
├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/checkout/shipping
│   ├── Body: shipping address JSON
│   └── ✅ Assertion
├── ⏱️ Timer (15000-30000ms)
├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/checkout/payment
│   ├── Body: payment details (use test cards!)
│   └── ✅ Assertion
├── ⏱️ Timer (10000-20000ms)
├── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/orders
│   └── ✅ Assertion (201)
├── ⏱️ Timer (5000-10000ms)
└── 🎯 HTTP GET /api/orders/confirmation
    └── ✅ Assertion (contains order number)

=========================================================================
TEARDOWN THREAD GROUP - Cleanup
=========================================================================

📁 Teardown Thread Group
├── Number of Threads: 1
├── Ramp-up: 1
├── Loop Count: 1
└── Comments: Clean up test data

Samplers:
├── 🎯 HTTP DELETE /api/test/users - Delete all test users
├── ✅ Assertion (200)
├── 🎯 HTTP DELETE /api/test/products - Delete test products
├── ✅ Assertion (200)
└── 🎯 HTTP POST /api/test/cleanup - Final cleanup

=========================================================================
LOAD PROFILE SUMMARY
=========================================================================

Load Over Time:

Time 0-60s:  Ramp-up New Visitors (0-200 users)
Time 60-120s: Ramp-up New Visitors (200-400) + Returning start
Time 120-180s: All groups ramping, load increasing
Time 180-300s: Peak load - all 1000 users active
Time 300-600s: Sustained peak load
Time 600s+:    Tests complete, teardown runs

Total Requests Estimate:
- New Visitors: 400 users × 3 loops × 5 requests = 6,000
- Returning: 350 × 4 × 8 = 11,200
- Buyers: 200 × 2 × 7 = 2,800
- Checkout: 50 × 1 × 9 = 450
- Setup/Teardown: ~1,000

Total: ~21,450 requests
Duration: ~10 minutes peak + ramp-up

=========================================================================
KEY METRICS TO MONITOR
=========================================================================

Per Thread Group:
├── Response times (avg, 95th, 99th percentile)
├── Error rates
├── Throughput (requests/sec)
└── Active thread count

Overall:
├── Server CPU/Memory
├── Database connections
├── Network bandwidth
└── Error distribution

Success Criteria:
├── Error rate < 1%
├── 95th percentile response < 3 seconds
├── All assertions pass
└── No server crashes

=========================================================================
"Realistic user simulation is the key to meaningful performance tests."
=========================================================================
```

content.title: Thread Group Configuration Cheat Sheet
content.content:
**📊 QUICK REFERENCE**

**Formula for users per second:**
`users/sec = threads / ramp-up`

**Formula for total requests:**
`total = threads × loops × samplers`

**Recommended ramp-up:**
`ramp-up = threads` (or longer for gentle start)

**Error handling by test type:**
- Load/Stress: Continue
- Functional: Stop Test
- Smoke: Stop Thread
- Debug: Continue

**Same user option:**
- ✓ For logged-in sessions
- ✗ For anonymous users
- ✓ When cookies/session needed

**Scheduler usage:**
- Use duration for soak tests
- Use loops for predictable totals
- Both for flexible control

**Thread Group types:**
- Setup: 1 thread, 1 loop
- Main: as needed
- Teardown: 1 thread, 1 loop

**Golden rule:** Start small, observe, then increase!

questions.question: Why are my threads not reaching the expected count?
questions.answer:
**Possible causes and solutions:**

1. **Ramp-up too long for test duration**
   - If test ends before ramp-up completes, threads never reach peak
   - Solution: Ensure test runs longer than ramp-up

2. **Infinite loop without duration**
   - Threads will run forever
   - Solution: Add scheduler duration or finite loops

3. **Memory issues**
   - Too many threads for available memory
   - Solution: Reduce threads or increase heap

4. **Threads stopping due to errors**
   - Error handling set to "Stop Thread"
   - Solution: Check for errors, change to "Continue"

questions.question: How do I know if my ramp-up is correct?
questions.answer:
**Check these indicators:**

✅ Good ramp-up:
- Server metrics increase gradually
- No spike at beginning
- Response times stable during ramp-up
- Throughput increases smoothly

❌ Too fast:
- Server CPU spikes immediately
- Errors at start of test
- Response time jumps

❌ Too slow:
- Test takes too long
- Not reaching target load in reasonable time
- Wasting test execution time

**Rule of thumb:**
- 1-2 users/second for gentle load
- 5-10 users/second for normal load
- 20+ users/second for spike tests

questions.question: Why are my test results inconsistent between runs?
questions.answer:
**Common causes:**

1. **Different thread start times**
   - Ramp-up causes different users to start at different times
   - Solution: Ensure you're comparing like-for-like

2. **Server variability**
   - Cache states, other users, background jobs
   - Solution: Multiple runs, average results

3. **Test data differences**
   - Different data each run
   - Solution: Use same data sets

4. **Network conditions**
   - Varying latency
   - Solution: Run in same environment

5. **JMeter machine variability**
   - Other processes, memory
   - Solution: Dedicated load generator
